(pp. 64-65, runs over the page break); (16a-d) p. 66; Table 1 'Fuzhou citation tones' p. 50. Chen & Norman 1965, Lesson 1 note 1 'Stress', printed Lesson 1-12 to 1-13 (scan).
catalog_quote: [pp. 64-65] First, the final syllable is the head of the disyllabic foot, and the foot is the head of the PrWd. Therefore, the final syllable is the strongest syllable in each PrWd. The non-final syllable(s) are either the non-headed syllable of the foot, or the unfooted syllable(s) in the PrWd. In both cases, the non-final syllables are relatively weak in the PrWd domain. The strong status ensures feature stability while the weak status leads to feature changes. That is why the syllables in the final position of a TSD always retain their citation tones, but the syllables in the non-final position(s) of a TSD undergo tone sandhi. ... Third, the unfooted weak syllable(s) dominated by the PrWd are even less prominent than the non-headed syllable of the foot. Therefore, the unfooted syllable(s) lose their citation tones, and default low tones (Tone21s) are inserted after the loss of tones. [p. 62] Her results show that the initial syllable in a disyllabic word reduces 2/3 length compared to its citation form, whereas the final syllable reduces less than 1/3 length compared to its citation form. This result indicates that the two syllables in a disyllabic word have different degrees of prominence. [fn. 13] Therefore, the final syllable is more prominent than the initial syllable.
world_status: statement found in an open source
sweep_summary: Min Dong (Fuzhou) is not in the catalog. Three title-hits: (1) Chan 1985 UW dissertation 'Fuzhou Phonology: A Non-Linear Analysis of Tone and Stress' -- directly about Fuzhou stress, but only available via ProQuest/UMI (author's OSU page confirms; no open copy anywhere probed); high acquisition priority, together with her 1984 UWWPL article 'Stress and vowel quality changes in the Fuzhou dialect' (8: 19-38). (2) Zhao & Bao 2024 review of You 2020 (Routledge prosodic-phonology monograph on Fuzhou sandhi domains) -- paywalled, one-line abstract; low priority (the book itself would be medium). (3) Chen 2019, Language and Linguistics 20(1), CC BY -- downloaded and read; pp. 62-64 state that Fuzhou prosodic words end in a right-headed disyllabic foot, the final syllable being the strongest (retains citation tone/vowel/weight) and all non-final syllables weak, citing Wright 1983 duration data and M. Chan 1985 / Jiang-King / L. Chan 1998. Best statement read: Chen 2019 p. 64 (fixed final prominence, tone-sandhi-diagnosed); no catalog source to supersede.

new_statements.second_reader_evidence: The quotation was checked again. Opened (39 pp., text; Chen, Aishu 2019, Language and Linguistics 20(1): 46-84, doi:10.1075/lali.00029.che; landing page saved as states "CC BY 4.0 license"). The quoted passage is present verbatim at §4.2.1 'The structure of the prosodic word', printed p. 64 (p. 19), paragraph beginning "The structures of the PrWds in (15) provide an account for the three-way distinction of tonal behavior. First, the final syllable is the head of the disyllabic foot, and the foot is the head of the PrWd. Therefore, the final syllable is the strongest syllable in each PrWd.."; the last clause "..but the syllables in / the non-final position(s) of a TSD undergo tone sandhi." r…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Fuzhou is a tone language with a disyllabic right-headed foot: the last syllable of a disyllabic word (and of every prosodic word / tone-sandhi domain of 2-4 syllables) is the prominent one; it keeps its citation tone and its full duration, while non-final syllables are weak, undergo tone sandhi (penult) or lose their tone to a default low tone 21 (antepenult and earlier). Chen p. 62 and fn. 13 ground the word-level claim in Wright's (1983) durations (initial syllable of a disyllabic word shortens by about 2/3, the final by less than 1/3): 'the final syllable is more prominent than the initial syllable'.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not stated. Chen distinguishes two grades of weakness: the penultimate (non-head of the foot) keeps a sandhi tone; unfooted antepenultimate syllables are 'even less prominent' and lose their tone (p. 65). No secondary prominence is posited, and iterative footing is explicitly excluded ((16c), p. 66).
new_statements.exceptions: None for position. Monosyllabic prosodic words are handled by footing the syllable with an empty syllable in phrase-final/pre-pause position (§4.3). Chen & Norman 1965 (pedagogical, Lesson 1-12/13) add a three-degree stress system (weak = toneless syllables, contrastive = extra loudness, normal) without any positional rule.
new_statements.domain_note: Prominence is stated for the prosodic word (PrWd), which Chen equates with the tone-sandhi domain (2-4 syllables) and which can span verb-object phrases, not only lexical words; the disyllabic-word claim (p. 62) rests on Wright 1983's acoustic durations and on the tone-sandhi asymmetry (initial syllable changes, final keeps its citation tone). 'Stress' is expressed as foot headedness/prominence in a tone language; the paper uses 'prominence' rather than 'stress' for Fuzhou.
new_statements.identity_note: All three opened sources describe the Fuzhou (Foochow) city dialect, the prestige variety of Min Dong: Chen 2019 analyses Fuzhou; Chen & Norman 1965 state (Introduction) that the book "represents the speech of a literate person from the city of Foochow"; Norman 1971 describes the Foochow city dialect.

new_statements.quote: Each PrWd contains only one disyllabic right-headed foot. The foot is the head of the PrWd, and it stands on the right edge of the PrWd. [...] First, the final syllable is the head of the disyllabic foot, and the foot is the head of the PrWd. Therefore, the final syllable is the strongest syllable in each PrWd. The non-final syllable(s) are either the non-headed syllable of the foot, or the unfooted syllable(s) in the PrWd. In both cases, the non-final syllables are relatively weak in the PrWd domain. The strong status ensures feature stability while the weak status leads to feature changes.
new_statements.citation: Chen, Aishu (2019). Interactions between prosody and morphosyntax in Fuzhou VO phrases. Language and Linguistics 20(1): 46-84.
new_statements.locator: pp. 62 (ex. 13 and following paragraph) and 64 (ex. 15 and following paragraph)
new_statements.reading: Fuzhou (Min Dong) word-level prominence is fixed on the final syllable of the prosodic word / tone-sandhi domain: a right-headed disyllabic foot at the right edge, with all preceding syllables weak. Evidence is metrical-phonological (final syllable keeps citation tone, vowel quality and weight; non-final syllables undergo sandhi and weight reduction) plus Wright's (1983) duration measurements; the author attributes the right-headed-foot analysis to Wright 1983, M. Chan 1985, Jiang-King 1995-1999 and L. Chan 1998. It is an analytic statement in a tone language, not a field description of audible stress, so a catalog's classification would be 'final / right-edge prominence (metrical, tone-sandhi-diagnosed)'. Chan 1985 (ProQuest-only) is the primary source and would be the better citation if acquired.

tone_statements.quote: Fuzhounese has seven citation tones, as given in Table II, that occur freely in the final position of a tone sandhi domain. The tonal inventory includes two high level tones—checked (/5/) and unchecked (/44/); three falling tones—high (/51/), mid (/32/), and low (/21/); a low rising tone (/24/); and a low rise-fall (/241/). Tones can be organized into two categories (or registers), referred to here as Set A and Set B, according to their participation in tone-vowel interaction and presence of non-modal phonation …

sources.note: Lesson 1, note 1 'Stress', printed pp. Lesson 1-12 to 1-13 (pp. 19-20): 'There are three degrees of stress in the Foochow dialect. a) Weak stress. Syllables which have no discernible tone contour are said to have weak stress; it is shown by the absence of any tone mark.. b) Contrastive stress.. characterized by extra loudness and increased tonal range.. c) Normal stress. Any syllable not carrying weak stress or contrastive stress will be considered to have normal stress.' No positional rule; weak-stressed (neutral-tone) syllables are enclitic and preceded by plus juncture (Lesson 6-17/18).

sources.note: First comprehensive acoustic survey of Fuqing tones and vowels, 14 speakers: SEVEN citation tones incl. FOUR falling contours -- the two higher falls differ in pitch height, the two mid falls differ in length and carry distinct phonation types, the lowest fall is a pure low [+LOW] tone; six vowel-height sets; tone-conditioned vowel alternation (bianyun) via height contrast and diphthongization, with a hypothesized phonation correlate.
